chapters.title: Chapter 2: Economic Terms an Angel Must Negotiate

children.text: Five years after Rohan wired his ₹20 lakh into ChaiCart, the company is still standing. It has not shut down. It has also not been acquired, has not gone public, and has no exit in sight. It is simply a mid-sized business, neither a failure nor a success story, with Rohan's money locked inside it. Every clause covered so far in this course assumes an exit eventually happens. This lesson covers the one clause built for what happens when it does not.

body.text: A redemption or buyback right is downside insurance for the scenario everyone hopes never happens: a company that neither fails nor exits, just stalls. It matters least when a startup is doing brilliantly or badly, and matters most in the long, quiet middle where most startups actually spend their time.

children.text: gives the investor a way to force cash out of the company, or out of the founders directly, after a fixed waiting period with no exit event, instead of holding shares indefinitely with no way to sell them.

markDefs.definition: A contractual right letting an investor require the company, or separately the founders, to buy back their shares for cash, typically after a fixed period has passed with no exit event.

children.text: "Clause 18, Buyback (illustrative wording): If no Exit Event has occurred within 5 (five) years from the date of Closing, the Investor shall have the right, exercisable by written notice, to require the Company to purchase all or part of the Investor's CCPS (or the equity shares into which they have converted) at a price equal to the higher of (a) the Original Issue Price plus a preferred return of 12% per annum, compounded annually, from the date of investment; or (b) the Fair Market Value of such shares as determined by an independent registered valuer, subject to applicable law."

body.caption: The cost-plus-return leg of a redemption clause, where r is the preferred return and n is the number of years held.

body.title: Pricing Rohan's Buyback
body.prompt: Using Clause 18 above, if ChaiCart never has an exit event and Rohan invokes his buyback after exactly 5 years, what does the cost-plus-return leg of his redemption price come to, in ₹ lakh? (Round to two decimal places.)
body.explanation: ₹20 lakh × (1.12)^5 = ₹20 lakh × 1.7623 ≈ ₹35.25 lakh. Rohan would take this figure or the independently assessed Fair Market Value, whichever is higher.

body.caption: Which price wins: Rohan takes whichever is higher

cells: Original investment compounded at the agreed rate, here 12% p.a.
When ChaiCart has grown slowly or stagnated, and Fair Market Value is close to or below what Rohan put in
An independent valuer's assessment of what the shares are worth today
When ChaiCart has grown well but still has not had a real exit event

children.text: Recall from Lesson 1.2 that a CCPS must be compulsorily and mandatorily convertible into equity to qualify as equity under India's foreign investment rules. A share that can instead be redeemed for cash starts to look like debt, which risks pulling the whole instrument out of the FDI-friendly equity regime and into stricter external borrowing rules, exactly the trap that applies to CCDs.

body.text: This is exactly why Indian term sheets rarely build a cash redemption feature directly into the CCPS itself. Instead, the clause is usually structured as a separate obligation on the company (a statutory buyback of the shares once converted, or of the CCPS where resident investors are involved) or on the founders personally (a promoter put option in the shareholders' agreement), rather than as a feature baked into the preference share.

children.text: When ChaiCart itself buys back Rohan's shares, it has to follow Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013. The rules exist to stop a company from paying out cash it does not actually have.

stats.label: Annual buyback ceiling
stats.context: Across all buybacks in a financial year, under Section 68

stats.label: Funding sources allowed
stats.value: Free reserves, securities premium, fresh share issue

stats.label: Post-buyback debt-equity ratio
stats.context: A further constraint on how much a company can buy back

body.text: Here is the trap that catches investors: a company that is struggling enough to still be sitting on Rohan's cheque five years later, with no exit, often has accumulated losses and no free reserves or securities premium left. Section 68 does not allow a buyback funded by fresh borrowing. A redemption clause can be perfectly valid on paper and still be legally impossible to execute, precisely in the scenario where an investor most wants to use it.

children.text: The Promoter Put: A Personal Backstop

works around the company's reserve constraint by making the buyback a personal promise from Ananya and Vikram, not from ChaiCart. It sits in the shareholders' agreement as an ordinary contractual obligation, not as a feature of the shares, so Section 68 never applies to it.

markDefs.definition: A personal contractual obligation on a company's founders to buy an investor's shares for cash if the company itself cannot, agreed separately in the shareholders' agreement.

body.title: Company buyback vs promoter put: two very different backstops

columns.label: Company Buyback (Section 68)
points: Legal obligation sits with the company itself
Must be funded from free reserves, securities premium or a fresh share issue, never borrowed money
Capped at 25% of paid-up capital plus free reserves in a financial year
Practically unavailable if the company has no distributable reserves, common for a struggling early-stage startup

columns.label: Promoter Put Option
points: Personal contractual obligation on the founders, agreed in the SHA, not a feature of the shares themselves
Not constrained by Section 68 or the company's reserves, since it is the founders' personal money
Enforced through a civil claim for breach of contract, not automatic
Real-world value depends entirely on whether the founders actually have the personal wealth to pay

body.text: A promoter put is a promise from two individuals, not a company balance sheet. Winning a breach of contract claim against Ananya and Vikram is one thing. Actually collecting from them, if their personal wealth is tied up the same startup that just failed to grow, is another.

body.title: The Buyback That Couldn't Happen
body.scenario: Five years after investing, Rohan invokes his redemption right. ChaiCart has survived but never had a proper exit, has accumulated losses on its books, and has no free reserves or securities premium left to draw on. Its accounts show it would need to borrow money to pay Rohan anything close to the ₹35.25 lakh his clause calculates.
body.prompt: Can ChaiCart lawfully buy back Rohan's shares right now? What are Rohan's realistic options?
body.modelAnswer: No. Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013 does not allow a company to fund a share buyback with borrowed money, and without free reserves or securities premium, ChaiCart cannot lawfully complete the buyback Rohan is asking for, however clearly his term sheet promises it. Rohan's realistic options are: wait until ChaiCart accumulates enough distributable reserves and negotiate a partial or staged buyback; check whether his SHA also gives him a personal promoter put against Ananya and Vikram, and pursue that separately, understanding it depends on their personal ability to pay; use the redemption clause as leverage in ChaiCart's next funding round, for instance asking incoming investors to fund a partial redemption as a closing condition; or, as a last resort, pursue a breach of contract claim, recognising that litigation is slow, costly, and does not guarantee that the money actually exists to collect.

body.title: What Blocks the Buyback
body.question: Which of the following would prevent ChaiCart's board from executing a valid buyback under Section 68, even if Rohan's redemption clause has been triggered?
options: The buyback is being funded out of ChaiCart's securities premium account
The board approved a buyback of an amount within 10% of paid-up capital plus free reserves, without a shareholder special resolution
ChaiCart has no free reserves or securities premium and would have to borrow the funds to pay Rohan
ChaiCart's Articles of Association expressly authorise buybacks
body.explanation: Buybacks under the Companies Act, 2013 must be funded from free reserves, securities premium, or the proceeds of a fresh share issue, never from borrowed money. A board-approved buyback within 10% of paid-up capital plus free reserves is actually a valid shortcut that skips the special resolution requirement, and Articles authorisation is simply a precondition. The absence of any lawful funding source is what actually stops the buyback.

body.label: Redemption gets more common as you move upstream
body.value: Rare in angel rounds, standard in growth and PE deals
body.context: Early-stage Indian angel and seed term sheets often skip redemption entirely, since a young company is unlikely to have the free reserves to fund one. Growth-stage and private equity deals build it in far more often, usually alongside stronger promoter guarantees and more sophisticated financial covenants.

cards.definition: A contractual right letting the investor require the company, or separately the founders, to buy back their shares for cash, typically after a fixed period with no exit event.
A minimum annual rate of return, often 12% to 15%, used to calculate a redemption price as the original investment compounded over the holding period.

The Companies Act, 2013 route for a company to lawfully repurchase its own shares, funded only from free reserves, securities premium, or fresh share proceeds, and capped at 25% of paid-up capital plus free reserves in a year.
A personal contractual obligation on the founders to buy an investor's shares if the company cannot, agreed separately in the shareholders' agreement.
The practical limit on any statutory buyback: a company with no distributable profits or reserves cannot lawfully fund one, whatever its term sheet promises.

points: A redemption or buyback right is downside protection for the scenario where a startup neither fails nor exits, just stalls, which is common among Indian startups.
A typical redemption clause pays the investor the higher of a cost-plus-preferred-return calculation or fair market value, after a fixed waiting period with no exit event.

Because CCPS must be compulsorily convertible to qualify as equity under FEMA, Indian term sheets usually route redemption through a separate company buyback or a personal promoter put, rather than building cash redemption into the share itself.

A company-level buyback under Section 68 can only be funded from free reserves, securities premium or a fresh share issue, never borrowed money, and is capped at 25% of paid-up capital plus free reserves in a year.
A struggling company with no distributable reserves cannot lawfully complete a buyback, whatever the term sheet says, exactly when an investor is most likely to want one.
A promoter put option adds a personal backstop from the founders, but its real value depends entirely on whether the founders actually have the money to honour it.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal or investment advice. ChaiCart, Rohan, Ananya and Vikram are fictional and used for illustration, and the clause language and figures shown are illustrative rather than a template for a real transaction. Redemption rights, buyback mechanics and their enforceability depend heavily on the specific drafting and the company's financial position, and should be reviewed by a qualified lawyer and chartered accountant before you rely on them. Startup investments are high risk, illiquid, and can result in the loss of your entire capital.
